posts.quote: I hid a spare key so I'd never get locked out. I hid it so well I've now been locked out twice, standing in the yard, guessing.
posts.caption: The fake rock was too obvious, so in April I got clever. That was my first mistake. I remember standing on the porch thinking nobody in a million years would look there, and I was right, because nobody now includes me. Last Tuesday at 6:40 I was in the front yard in my work shoes, lifting a ceramic frog, two flowerpots and a very offended gnome while the neighbor pretended to check his mail for nine straight minutes. It was under none of them. My sister finally texted me where I'd told her it was. The birdhouse. I had completely forgotten we own a birdhouse.
posts.first: My mother kept her spare key in a coffee can in the garage for thirty-one years and never once forgot where it was. I have tried four hiding spots since spring. The current one is a secret even from me, which my husband says is the whole point of hiding it. It is not.

posts.quote:
10am: I could sleep for a week.
2pm: Begging for a nap.
6pm: Barely operational.
12:32am: Whatever happened to the band Duran Duran?
posts.caption: All day I was tired. Not regular tired, the kind where you stand in the pantry and forget what a cracker is. At two I put my head down on the kitchen table for what I called a minute. At six I made dinner mostly with my eyes closed. Then I got into bed at 9:45, and my brain sat straight up like somebody rang a bell. By 12:32 I was three articles deep on the bassist's solo career. I now know where every member of that band lives. I still don't know where my car keys are.
posts.first: My husband rolled over around one and asked why the phone was glowing. I told him I was researching the eighties. He said okay and went back to sleep. In the morning he asked if I'd slept well. I told him I'd learned a lot.

posts.quote: I’ve reached the age where walking past a bathroom without stopping feels like a reckless decision.
posts.caption: We drove two hours to my niece's graduation party in June, and I stopped at every rest area like it was a scheduled tour. By the third one my husband started announcing them. Coming up on your left, ladies and gentlemen. I did not find this as funny as he did. Here's what nobody tells you. It's not that you need to go. It's that you might need to go in forty minutes, and the next exit is a gas station with the key chained to a hubcap. I am not gambling on that. I've seen what happens to people who gamble.
posts.first: Saturday at the outlet mall I walked right past a clean, empty restroom because I was in a hurry. Eleven minutes later I was speed-walking through a shoe store with my purse clutched to my chest. I've learned nothing. I will do it again next month.

posts.quote: I bought three bags of Halloween candy early so I'd be ready. I was not ready. I'm on my fourth bag and it isn't even Halloween.
posts.first: The first bag lasted until a Thursday. I told myself I was testing it for quality, which is a real job somebody has to do. By the third bag I was hiding the wrappers at the bottom of the trash like a teenager. I am fifty-three years old.

posts.quote: People worry about me being single. Meanwhile I’m starfished across the whole bed, remote in hand, living my best thermostat-controlled life. I’ll be fine.
posts.caption: At Thanksgiving my aunt leaned over the sweet potatoes and asked, very gently, if I was ever going to meet someone. Like I'd lost my umbrella. I told her I had met someone. Every night at 9:30 I meet the exact middle of a queen-size mattress, and we get along beautifully. Nobody steals the covers. Nobody snores. Nobody touches the thermostat, which stays at 68 because I said so. She patted my hand like I was being brave. I was not being brave. I was thinking about the bed. I'd been thinking about it since the turkey.
posts.first: I bought the good sheets last spring, the ones that cost more than my first car payment. Then I bought four extra pillows just because there was room. Last night I woke up diagonal with the remote under my cheek. Best sleep of the month.

posts.quote: Life is full of questions I’ll never get answers to. The single shoe on the side of the highway is at the top of the list.
posts.caption: I've seen it on the interstate, on the county road past the dairy, and once on the exit ramp by the outlet mall. One shoe. Never two. Always just the one, lying there like it has somewhere to be. I've spent more time thinking about that shoe than about my retirement account. Did someone kick it out a window? Was it a toddler with a strong arm? Did somebody get home and only then notice they were walking funny? I've made my peace with not knowing most things in life. Not this. This one I'd still like answered.
posts.first: Last Tuesday it was a single white work boot on the shoulder near mile marker 112. Laced up. My sister and I talked about it for twenty minutes over dinner and got nowhere. She thinks it's the same boot following us around. I'm starting to agree.

posts.quote: I always wonder if one of my calls was ever recorded for training purposes. And more importantly, what exactly it trained them to do.
posts.caption: Wednesday I spent fifty-two minutes on hold with the cable company listening to the same eight seconds of saxophone. Every few minutes a very calm recording reminded me that this call may be recorded for training purposes. Good. By minute forty I had decided to give them something to train with. When a real person finally picked up, I was polite, clear, and extremely specific about my feelings. I said I understand it's not your fault three times, and I meant it twice. My bill went down eleven dollars. Somewhere out there, a new hire is listening to me and taking notes.
posts.first: My mother used to call the gas company with a pen and a legal pad and write down every name she talked to. She'd read them back at the end like a court stenographer. I didn't understand it as a kid. I have the legal pad now.

posts.quote: The older I get, the less I care what people think of me. I barely care what I think, and I’m stuck with me all day.
posts.caption: At thirty I changed my outfit three times for a neighborhood barbecue. At forty I still asked my sister if my haircut looked okay. Somewhere around fifty-two I went to the grocery store in my husband's flannel, my gardening clogs, and one earring, and didn't notice until the checkout line. The cashier noticed. She looked at the earring, then at me, then back at the earring. I looked right back at her and asked for paper instead of plastic. That was the day I knew. It's very freeing. I recommend it to anyone who still owns a lint roller.
posts.first: Last month a lady at church told me my hair was brave. Twenty years ago that would have kept me up all night. This time I said thank you, went home, and made a sandwich. I couldn't tell you what she was wearing.

posts.quote: I said I'd rest my eyes for a minute. That was at 7:40. The minute ended at 10:15.
posts.first: I woke up with the remote on my chest and the TV asking if I was still watching. I was not. Nobody was. My husband had covered me with a blanket and gone to bed. That's love at this age. A blanket and no questions.

posts.quote: Apparently getting through menopause takes more protein, more water, strength training, daily walks, eight hours of sleep, and less stress. Great. I was worried my to-do list wasn’t already long enough.
posts.caption: My doctor handed me a printed list at my last checkup. Front and back. Protein at every meal, eight glasses of water, lift weights three times a week, walk every day, sleep eight hours, and somehow, while doing all that, reduce stress. I read it in the parking lot. Then I read it again, because I thought I'd missed the part where someone comes over and does my laundry. I had not. So far I've managed the water. Mostly because I'm up at 3 a.m. anyway and the kitchen is right there. Baby steps.
posts.first: I bought a set of hand weights in purple because they were on sale. They're currently holding the pantry door open. My husband asked if I'd started strength training yet. I told him I carry the laundry basket upstairs twice a week. The weights have done less.

posts.quote: Back in my day, we called it “going outside” and nobody had to download an app to do it.
posts.caption: My granddaughter showed me an app last weekend that tracks your steps, your heart rate, and how many minutes you spend outdoors, and then gives you a little badge. A badge. For going outside. When I was nine, we went outside because that's where the bikes were. Nobody counted anything. My grandmother counted the tomatoes, but that was a different thing entirely. I told my granddaughter all this on the back step. She said it sounded nice. Then she checked how many minutes it had been. Eleven. She got a badge.
posts.first: I sat out on the back porch this morning for almost an hour. Watched a squirrel bury the same acorn three times, then dig it right back up. No app knew about it. Nobody gave me a badge. It was still the best hour of my week.

posts.quote: I don’t need anti-aging cream. I need anti-nonsense cream, applied daily to everyone around me.
posts.caption: The woman at the department store counter spent twenty minutes last Saturday explaining a serum to me. It had gold in it. Actual gold, she said, as if my face had been asking for jewelry. I let her finish because she was very sweet and clearly on commission. Then I told her my skin was fine and what I really needed was something for the people around me. Something you could rub on a coworker before a meeting. She laughed. I wasn't joking. I walked out with a free sample and a much clearer sense of the market gap.
posts.first: My aunt Ruth used nothing but cold cream and a strong opinion for sixty years and had the best skin in the family. She also had no patience for anyone. I've always thought those two things were related. I'm testing the theory.

rejected.caption: At my cousin's Labor Day cookout, a man I had known for eleven minutes told me to relax. I was holding a paper plate of potato salad and minding my own business by the cooler. It has been through two kitchen remodels, a wedding, and a timeshare presentation, and it has never once been asked to change. I explained this to him calmly. He went to go stand by the grill. My face, for the record, was perfectly relaxed the entire time he walked away.

rejected.quote: I raked the leaves once in 1998. The wind has been handling it ever since.
rejected.caption: There's a rake in my garage that I bought at a Sears that doesn't exist anymore. I used it one Saturday in October of 1998, made three beautiful piles, and watched a single gust of wind put every leaf back exactly where it started. I took that personally for about an hour. Then I took it as advice. Every fall since, the neighbors rake and bag and haul, and every spring my yard looks exactly like theirs. Nobody can tell the difference. The maple doesn't care either way.
